lesson.title: A Different Migration: Southern and Eastern Europeans Reshape America
lesson.summary: Beginning in the 1880s, millions of immigrants from Italy, Poland, Russia, and other parts of southern and eastern Europe arrived in the United States, differing in language, religion, and culture from earlier immigrant generations and filling the factories, mines, and mills built by American industrialization.
lesson.body:
The factories, mines, and railroads created during the Industrial Revolution in America needed an enormous and growing supply of labor. The rail network built across the country, symbolized by the completion of the Transcontinental Railroad in 1869, connected the port cities where immigrants arrived to the industrial cities and mining regions where jobs waited, distributing new arrivals across the country almost as soon as they landed.

Historians distinguish this era's arrivals as the new immigration, to separate them from the old immigration of earlier decades. Old immigration came largely from Britain, Ireland, Germany, and Scandinavia, and included many Protestants and Catholics whose backgrounds were relatively familiar to native born Americans. New immigration, which began accelerating in the 1880s and continued into the 1920s, came heavily from Italy, Poland, Russia, Austria-Hungary, Greece, and other parts of southern and eastern Europe, and included large numbers of Catholics, Jews, and Orthodox Christians who spoke languages unfamiliar to most Americans and often looked, dressed, and worshipped differently from earlier arrivals.

People left for a mix of reasons. Push factors included rural poverty and land shortages in places like southern Italy, and religious and political persecution, including violent pogroms against Jewish communities in the Russian Empire. Pull factors included the promise of industrial jobs, increasingly affordable and faster steamship travel across the Atlantic, and letters and remittances from relatives and neighbors who had already made the crossing.

The scale of this migration was immense. Roughly 20 million immigrants arrived in the United States between the 1880s and the 1920s, the large majority settling in industrial cities of the Northeast and Midwest, fueling the rapid growth of American cities described in the story of Urbanization.

Their arrival also provoked a strong nativist backlash. Many native born Americans, including many in the labor movement, viewed the new immigrants as racially or culturally inferior and feared they would depress wages by accepting lower pay. Calls grew for restrictions such as literacy tests, foreshadowing the sharp immigration quotas Congress would eventually impose in the 1920s.
